Citation / study title: Adsorption properties of tetracycline onto graphene oxide: equilibrium, kinetic and thermodynamic studies
Preparation/process reported: GO; source excerpt does not provide a full manufacturing cost or process inventory.
Experimental design and conditions: Methods report equilibrium tests using 25 mL TC solution (6–180 mg/L) in 50 mL flasks with GO suspension (20 mg/L), adjusted to pH 6–7 and incubated overnight. pH experiments used 2 mL GO suspension (20 mg/L) plus 4 mL TC (10–100 mg/L), pH 2–10; kinetics used 2 mL GO (20 mg/L) plus 4 mL TC (6–180 mg/L) at pH 3.6.
Observed result(s): Kinetic equilibrium is reported within 15 min. The paper also studied TC release/desorption across pH values and reports release up to 99.8%; this is not equivalent to validated repeated-cycle reuse.
Model-derived capacity / model fit: Langmuir fitted qmax reported as 322.43 mg/g at 298 K in the conclusion; abstract rounds this to 323 mg/g. D–R mean adsorption energy reported as 1.83 kJ/mol at 298 K.
Kinetics / isotherm: Pseudo-second-order fit reported; Langmuir described as best fit. Conditions differ between equilibrium, pH and kinetic experiments.
Mechanism evidence / author interpretati: Authors discuss π–π interaction, cation–π interactions and hydrophobic/dispersion effects; computational simulation also considered. Treat these as proposed/interpretive mechanisms, not directly measured force contributions.
Recovery / regeneration: Release/desorption investigated; release percentage up to 99.8% reported. No multi-cycle regeneration protocol was confirmed in the extracted sections.
Cost / feasibility evidence: No quantified cost, energy, synthesis yield or process inventory identified in the extracted article sections. Cost evidence: not established.
Source location within article: Abstract; Methods: “General Adsorption Experiments”; Results: pH/kinetics; Conclusions.
Extraction status: Full-text indexed content extracted; provisional inclusion
Caveats / next check: Do not directly compare fitted qmax with measured qe from other studies. Source gives qmax as 322.43 in conclusion and ~323 in abstract (rounding). Kinetic experiments were at pH 3.6; isotherm tests were described at pH 6–7.

Citation / study title: Adsorption of tetracycline antibiotics from an aqueous solution onto graphene oxide/calcium alginate composite fibers
Preparation/process reported: Prepared by freeze-drying; calcium chloride used as cross-linker between GO and sodium alginate.
Experimental design and conditions: Equilibrium: 25 mg adsorbent in 50 mL TC solutions, shaken 5 h at 25°C. pH tests: 10 mg adsorbent in 20 mL TC at 50 mg/L, pH 2–9. Dose tests: 5–30 mg in 20 mL TC at 50 mg/L. Kinetic test: 200 mg fibers in 400 mL TC at 50 mg/L.
Observed result(s): At initial TC 10 mg/L, equilibrium concentration was 1.2 mg/L and observed qe was 17.6 mg/g. At initial TC 60 mg/L, equilibrium concentration was 27.3 mg/L and observed qe was 65.4 mg/g. In the pH study, the highest reported removal was 56.8% at pH 6. At initial TC 50 mg/L, removal was 35.0% with 5 mg adsorbent and 69.4% with 30 mg.
Model-derived capacity / model fit: Langmuir fitted qmax = 131.6 mg/g at 25°C, R² = 0.9938. This is a fitted parameter, not observed uptake at C0=10 or 60 mg/L.
Kinetics / isotherm: Langmuir fit R² = 0.9938; paper reports pseudo-second-order kinetic fit and interprets uptake in terms of intraparticle diffusion.
Mechanism evidence / author interpretati: Authors propose hydrogen bonding and π–π stacking; electrostatic affinity is also mentioned. Mechanism should be treated as the authors’ interpretation unless supported by specific controls/characterization.
Recovery / regeneration: Fiber format enables solid–liquid separation by centrifugation in reported tests. No repeated-cycle regeneration study was identified in the extracted source sections.
Cost / feasibility evidence: No quantified cost inventory identified. Freeze-drying and calcium chloride cross-linking are reported preparation steps, but their monetary/energy burden is not calculated in the extracted paper sections.
Source location within article: Abstract; Methods §2.4; Results §§3.2.1–3.2.3; Table 1; Conclusions.
Extraction status: Full-text indexed content extracted; provisional inclusion
Caveats / next check: Do not treat pH-study removal percentage, measured qe and fitted qmax as interchangeable. A multi-cycle regeneration result was not found in the source sections extracted.

Citation / study title: Adsorption of Tetracycline with Reduced Graphene Oxide Decorated with MnFe2O4 Nanoparticles

Citation / study title: Graphene oxide/layered double hydroxide composite as highly efficient and recyclable adsorbent for removal of ciprofloxacin from aqueous phase
Preparation/process reported: LDH prepared by co-precipitation; GO and GO-ZnAlNi LDH composite synthesis includes hydrothermal ageing. Reagents include graphite and Ni, Zn, Al nitrate salts plus NaOH.
Experimental design and conditions: Batch design: 20 mL solution; CIP range 0.225–10 mg/L; composite dose 1–12 mg/L; pH 3–11; contact time 0–4 h; stirring 180 rpm. The paper gives q=(C0−Ct)V/W. At C0=1 mg/L, dose=10 mg/L, pH 7 and 60 min, its removal percentage is 84.84%. From the stated formula and these conditions, the implied qe is 84.84 mg/g (calculated from removal and dose; not a separately measured value).
Observed result(s): 84.84% removal at C0=1 mg/L, composite dose 10 mg/L, pH 7, 60 min. Five-cycle removal reportedly declines from 80.4% in cycle 1 to 27% in cycle 5.
Model-derived capacity / model fit: Capacity reporting is internally inconsistent: narrative gives 97.43 mg/g alongside 84.84% removal at C0=1 mg/L and dose=10 mg/L; abstract and Table 3 report 106.97/106.9 mg/g; elsewhere dose-series capacities are 88.89 mg/g at reported 64% removal and 77.95 mg/g at reported 73.86% removal. Using the paper's own equation, removal and dose pairs imply 84.84 mg/g, about 85.33 mg/g, and 61.55 mg/g respectively. Table 2 reports Freundlich and Temkin fit parameters (R² 0.95 and 0.90), not a verified Langmuir qmax. Treat all reported capacity values as unresolved pending source clarification.
Kinetics / isotherm: Freundlich model fit is reported as better than Langmuir; Freundlich R²=0.95 and Temkin R²=0.90 in the parameter table. Authors describe multi-site/multilayer adsorption.
Mechanism evidence / author interpretati: Authors propose π–π interactions and hydrogen bonding; kinetic-model interpretations include pseudo-first-order and Elovich, but model fit alone does not prove a microscopic mechanism.
Recovery / regeneration: Five reuse cycles studied; reported removal fell from 80.4% at cycle 1 to 27% at cycle 5. This is a substantial performance loss, despite the article’s generally positive reuse language.
Cost / feasibility evidence: Article discusses cost-effectiveness and easy-to-access materials qualitatively, but no quantified manufacturing cost, life-cycle assessment, or per-mass-contaminant cost is provided in extracted sections. Nitrate precursors/hydrothermal processing should be captured in any process-cost discussion.
Source location within article: Methods §§2.1–2.3; Results §§3.2.3, 3.5; Table 2, Table 3, Fig. 7; Conclusions.
Extraction status: Full text extracted; endpoint/capacity inconsistency flagged
Caveats / next check: Resolved part-way: article equation and stated C0/removal/dose permit mass-balance checks, but the source gives multiple incompatible capacities. Use only the stated condition-specific removal result (84.84%) plus explicit caveat; do not report an authoritative capacity for this material unless the authors/source supplementary data resolve it. Five-cycle reuse falls to 27% removal.

Citation / study title: Integration of magnetic graphene oxide and office waste paper-derived fibrillated cellulose into a composite adsorbent for effective tetracycline elimination
Preparation/process reported: GO made using modified Hummers method; magnetite attached to GO (same-mass mixing, ultrasound 360 W for 30 min). Experimental design and conditions: Batch tests: 15 mg composite in 30 mL solution (0.50 g/L base dose), 160 rpm, magnet used for separation. Dose-effect tests used C0(TC)=70 mg/L, contact time 960 min, pH varied 3–8 and dose range 0.50–1.17 g/L; pH 5 selected for subsequent tests.
Observed result(s): Observed qe in dose study was 93.36±3.85 mg/g at 0.50 g/L and 59.52±0.11 mg/g at 1.17 g/L. Removal efficiency decreased from 88.33% after cycle 1 to 75.38% after cycle 5.

Kinetics / isotherm: Sips model best fit; pseudo-second-order was the best-fitting kinetic model in the paper. The paper interprets the surface as heterogeneous; do not infer chemisorption from kinetic fit alone.
Mechanism evidence / author interpretati: FTIR/XPS before/after adsorption used to discuss interactions including hydrogen bonding, π–π interaction, and electrostatic effects. These are proposed based on characterization and solution pH/speciation.
Recovery / regeneration: Magnetic separation demonstrated; five adsorption–desorption cycles. Removal decreased by 12.95 percentage points, 88.33% to 75.38%.
Cost / feasibility evidence: Waste-paper origin is incidental to the selected graphene-composite scope, not a defining theme. No quantified cost inventory was extracted. Preparation is multi-step and includes strong acid hydrolysis, alkali treatment, oxidation/bleaching, magnetite synthesis, ultrasonication and 48 h freeze-drying; waste feedstock alone does not establish low total cost.
Source location within article: Methods §§2.3–2.8; Results §§3.2.1–3.2.6; Table 1, Table 2, Fig. 7, Fig. 8, Fig. 10, Fig. 11, Fig. 12.
Extraction status: Full-text extracted; provisional inclusion

Citation / study title: Carboxymethylcellulose functionalized magnetic graphene oxide for the efficient removal of tetracycline from aqueous media
Preparation/process reported: Article reports synthesis from electronic-waste-derived GO and functionalization with magnetic Fe3O4 and CMC; detailed reagent/process accounting still requires direct methods-table audit.
Experimental design and conditions: Batch tests in 100 mL flasks. Base/optimum removal test: C0(TC)=2 mg/L, 2 mg adsorbent in 20 mL (0.1 g/L), pH 5, 25°C, 250 rpm, 25 min. Dose series: 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10 mg in 20 mL at C0=2 mg/L. pH tests pH 2–10 at 25°C with 2 mg adsorbent and C0=2 mg/L. Concentration tests: C0=0.2–10 mg/L at pH 5, 2 mg adsorbent, 25°C. Isotherms are evaluated at 25, 40 and 50°C.
Observed result(s): At C0=2 mg/L, dose 0.1 g/L, pH 5, 25°C and 25 min, reported TC removal=96.04%. Mass-balance-derived qe = (2 mg/L × 0.9604)/(0.1 g/L) = 19.208 mg/g (calculated, not a directly quoted experimental qe). In the concentration series, removal declines from 99.43% at C0=0.2 mg/L to 44.99% at C0=10 mg/L. Ten-cycle reuse reportedly reduces removal from approximately 96% to 92%. Saturation magnetization=50.69 emu/g.
Model-derived capacity / model fit: Linear Langmuir qm: 45.5581 mg/g at 25°C (R²=0.9952), 51.4933 mg/g at 40°C (R²=0.9969), 54.7346 mg/g at 50°C (R²=0.9809). Non-linear Langmuir qm: 44.0051, 48.6490 and 48.4744 mg/g at 25, 40 and 50°C, respectively (R²=0.9569, 0.9895, 0.9425). Linear pseudo-second-order fitted qe=19.5008 mg/g (R²=0.9999); non-linear pseudo-second-order fitted qe=19.3522 mg/g. Do not treat these as direct observations.
Kinetics / isotherm: Langmuir isotherm and pseudo-second-order kinetics reported. Do not treat the PSO fit as independent proof of chemisorption.
Mechanism evidence / author interpretati: Authors attribute adsorption to hydrogen bonding, π–π interactions, and electrostatic forces; magnetic behaviour supports separation, not necessarily stronger adsorption by itself.
Recovery / regeneration: External magnetic separation followed by regeneration using methanol; ten cycles reportedly retain removal from about 96% to 92%.
Cost / feasibility evidence: No quantified total cost or energy inventory. Preparation from electronics waste involves graphite recovery and cleaning (aqua regia treatment, repeated washing), modified-Hummers oxidation using concentrated H2SO4/H3PO4 and KMnO4, H2O2 quench, HCl/water/ethanol washing, Fe salts, CMC and 2.0 M NaOH; subsequent 85°C treatment for 2 h and vacuum drying at 60°C for 18 h. The paper’s statement that the route is cost-effective is not a cost calculation. Methanol regeneration also has procurement, handling and waste-treatment implications.
Source location within article: Methods §§2.3–2.6; Results §§3.2.1–3.2.4; Table 2 kinetic parameters; Table 3 isotherm parameters; Table 4 comparison; §3.2.8 reusability; Conclusions.
Extraction status: Detailed indexed full-text extraction completed; provisional inclusion; model/temperature details clarified
Caveats / next check: The abstract's 54.73 mg/g is the linear Langmuir fit at 50°C. Standard 96.04% removal condition is 25°C and C0=2 mg/L, for which mass-balance-derived qe is ~19.21 mg/g. Table 4's q_m row lists 50°C and therefore should not be read as the 25°C optimum condition. Linear and nonlinear fit qm differ appreciably; name the fitting method in any comparison. Obtain SI if needed for exact cycle data.

Citation / study title: Performance of magnetic graphene oxide/diethylenetriaminepentaacetic acid nanocomposite for the tetracycline and ciprofloxacin adsorption in single and binary systems
Preparation/process reported: Primary indexed full text reports synthesis of GO, magnetic GO (Fe3O4/GO), then DTPA functionalization with EDC/NHS coupling. DDMGO surface has O/N-containing groups; DTPA carboxyl groups combine with GO amine groups to form amide bonds. Full reagent quantities/yield are not yet transcribed from an inspectable PDF page image.
Experimental design and conditions: Primary indexed full text: 25 mL conical flasks; shaking 150 rpm; about 2.28 mg DDMGO per reaction (~91.2 mg/L based on 25 mL). pH effects: initial antibiotic concentration 50 mg/L, 30°C. Kinetics: 50 mg/L, 30°C, 0–1560 min. Isotherms/thermodynamics: initial concentration 0–500 mg/L, pH 3.0, 293/303/313 K. Ionic-strength tests: NaCl 0–0.5 mol/L; background ions K+, Mg2+, Cl− and SO4^2− 0–0.1 mol/L. Binary tests: 50 mg/L TC with CIP 0–20 mg/L and 50 mg/L CIP with TC 0–20 mg/L. Regeneration: four consecutive cycles with 0.01 M NaOH; single 50 mg/L solutions and binary 50/10 mg/L combinations, 250 mL suspension, ~22.8 mg adsorbent, 24 h at 30°C and pH 3.0.
Observed result(s): Indexed primary text reports CIP sorption reaches equilibrium after about 1 h, while TC continues to increase and approaches a plateau at about 24 h; 24 h was chosen for equilibrium/isotherm tests. Exact directly observed qe at the kinetic-test conditions must be transcribed from Fig. 3 once a visually inspectable PDF is available. The primary paper states pseudo-second-order fitted qe values were closer to experimental values, but this is not itself a direct qexp value.
Model-derived capacity / model fit: Primary text explicitly identifies 294.12 mg/g (TC) and 111.73 mg/g (CIP) as qe values calculated from the pseudo-second-order equation and says they were closer to experimental values. These are kinetic-model-fitted qe values at the kinetic conditions, not verified Langmuir qmax values. Equilibrium isotherm data fit Freundlich better than other tested models; do not call these two figures isotherm qmax. Secondary reviews reproduce them as 'adsorption capacity', which is less precise than the primary paper's parameter definition.
Kinetics / isotherm: Linear pseudo-first-order and pseudo-second-order kinetic models used. Pseudo-second-order fitted qe values: TC 294.12 mg/g, CIP 111.73 mg/g. Freundlich model described equilibrium data better. The exact kinetic rate constants, R² and experimental qe require numeric table/figure transcription from a readable copy.
Mechanism evidence / author interpretati: The primary abstract attributes adsorption primarily to π–π interaction, hydrogen bonding and amidation; cation–π interaction is proposed for TC and electrostatic interaction for CIP. SEM/TEM, XRD, BET, FTIR, XPS and zeta-potential measurements were used; surface area 176 m²/g, average pore diameter 3.8 nm, pore volume 0.24 cm³/g. Treat mechanistic assignments as author interpretations supported by a combination of characterization and tests, not direct partitioning of force contributions.
Recovery / regeneration: Four successive adsorption–desorption cycles tested using 0.01 M NaOH as eluent. Permanent magnet used to separate DDMGO from solution. Exact cycle-by-cycle retention percentages remain to be read from the original figure/table.
Cost / feasibility evidence: No quantified cost inventory or energy/cost per antibiotic removed has been confirmed. Preparation involves GO oxidation, Fe3O4 magnetic functionalization and DTPA/EDC/NHS coupling; materials include DTPA, EDC, NHS, graphite, FeCl3·6H2O and FeSO4·7H2O. Magnetic separation is an operational benefit but not proof of low total cost.

PDF page-image check failed because publisher/institution PDF fetch timed out, so exact table/figure transcription remains pending.
Extraction status: Primary indexed full-text text extracted; detailed conditions and parameter identity clarified; visual PDF/table audit still pending

Citation / study title: Exploring the Adsorption Efficiency of Sulfonated Graphene Oxide for Ciprofloxacin Removal from Aqueous Solution: Insights from Density Functional Theory, Kinetics, Thermodynamics, and Reusability
Preparation/process reported: Modified improved-Hummers route: 3.0 g graphite flakes treated with a 9:1 mixture of 18.4 mol/L H2SO4 and 14.6 mol/L H3PO4; 18.0 g KMnO4 added at 30°C and stirred 24 h; then 400 mL cold water and 3 mL 30% H2O2 added; sequential washing with 7.7 mol/L HCl, deionized water, ethanol and diethyl ether; oven dried at 60°C. Product yield/cost not reported.
Experimental design and conditions: Base kinetic test: 50 mL of 50 μmol/L CIP, 0.2 g/L SGO, pH 4.0, 25°C, 150 rpm; aliquots from 0–240 min. Salt tests with 0.1 M Na2SO4, K2SO4, CaSO4 and MgSO4.
Observed result(s): Table 1 gives experimental qe values 45.45, 121.06, 237.12, 326.06 and 402.58 μmol/g at C0=10,25,50,75,100 μmol/L, respectively. At C0=50 μmol/L, pH 4 and 25°C, qe(exp)=237.12 μmol/g (~78.6 mg/g). pH-test peak is reported as 238.48 μmol/g at pH 4.0. Dose increase 0.06→0.4 g/L increased removal 60.10→97.98%, while qe fell 495.96→121.29 μmol/g. Salt effects decrease uptake in order Ca2+ > Mg2+ > K+ > Na+.
